title: The distribution of eccentricities in random regular graphs
authors: Dor Lev-Ari, Ofer Biham, Eytan Katzav
abstract: We derive a closed-form analytical expression for the distribution of eccentricities (DoE) in random regular graphs (RRGs) that consist of $N$ nodes of degree $c$. The DoE is given by the tail distribution $P(E > \ell) \simeq 1 - \exp \left[ - \exp \left( - \frac{ e^{b \ell} - μ}β \right) \right]$, where the distance $\ell$ takes integer values, $b = \ln (c-1)$ is the shape parameter, $β= \frac{c-2}{c} N$ is the scale parameter and $μ= \frac{c-2}{c} N \ln N$ is the location parameter. By providing the full distribution rather than a single characteristic length scale, we present a detailed view of the large-scale structure. In spite of the fact that the degrees of all the nodes are the same, their eccentricities exhibit non-trivial variations. We derive a closed-form expression for the mean eccentricity, which is given by $\langle E \rangle \simeq \frac{\ln N}{\ln (c-1)} + \frac{\ln \ln N}{\ln (c-1)} - \frac{ \ln c - \ln (c-2) }{ \ln (c-1) } + \frac{1}{2}$. We calculate the mode of the DoE, which exhibits a staircase profile as a function of the network size. Interestingly, the mode is given by $E_{\rm mode} ={\rm Round} \left( \langle E \rangle \right)$, where ${\rm Round}( x )$ is the nearest integer to $x$. We also calculate the variance ${\rm Var}(E)$ and show that it exhibits oscillations as a function of the network size $N$. The results presented in this paper may serve as benchmarks for algorithmic approaches to eccentricity calculations in large sparse networks. The eccentricities are important in practical applications such as broadcasting and global dissemination, where the network performance is determined by the longest delay times.
summary: This paper provides rigorous analytical results for the distribution of eccentricities in Random Regular Graphs. By deriving closed-form expressions for key statistical measures like the mean and variance, it offers a detailed understanding of network structure based on graph theory principles. The methods developed using extreme value statistics are valuable benchmarks for analyzing global properties in large complex systems.
main_problem: The primary goal is deriving a closed-form analytical expression for the distribution of eccentricities (DoE) in random regular graphs (RRGs). This provides a detailed view of the large-scale structure beyond just characteristic length scales.
main_result: A closed-form tail distribution $P(E > \ell)$ is derived, along with asymptotic expressions for the mean eccentricity $\langle E angle$ and variance $	ext{Var}(E)$. The mode is found to be close to the rounded value of the mean eccentricity.
method: The analysis employs Extreme Value Theory (EVT) and utilizes tail-sum formulas combined with approximations like the Euler-Maclaurin formula to analyze moments ($\langle E angle, \langle E^2 angle$).
model_or_system: The model is a Random Regular Graph (RRG) consisting of $N$ nodes, where every node has a fixed degree $c$. Eccentricity quantifies the maximum shortest path distance from any node to all others.
key_observables: Distribution of eccentricities ($P(E > \ell)$), Mean eccentricity ($\langle E angle$), Mode of DoE ($E_{	ext{mode}}$), and Variance ($	ext{Var}(E)$).
important_parameters: Number of nodes $N$, constant degree $c$ (with $c \ge 3$). The analysis is focused on the large $N$ limit.
main_assumptions: The derivations rely on approximations derived from the tail distribution of shortest path lengths and assume that correlations between distances can be managed or neglected in the asymptotic limit.
figures_summary: Figures compare analytical predictions ($	imes$, $+$) against simulation results ($\circ$) for the mode ($E_{	ext{mode}}$) and variance ($	ext{Var}(E)$) as a function of network size $N$ for fixed degree $c=5$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the tail distribution using EVT, then deriving closed-form expressions for higher moments like $\langle E^2 angle$, and finally analyzing the resulting variance and mode behavior as functions of network size.
why_interesting: While focused on graph theory, the mathematical techniques used—analyzing extreme value statistics (eccentricity) in large complex systems—are highly relevant to characterizing rare events or global properties in quantum many-body systems or disordered lattices.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Analytical results (×) for the distribution of eccentricities P(E > ℓ) of nodes in RRGs that consist of nodes of degree c = 5 and network sizes of (a) N = 160; (b) N = 242; (c) N = 272; (d) N = 296; (e) N = 322 and (f) N = 440. The analytical results, obtained from Eq. (14), are in reasonable agreement with the results obtained from computer simulations (◦), where the deviations are due to ﬁnite-size eﬀects. The simulation results were averaged over 20 network instances. For N = 160 the eccentricity of essentially all the nodes is E = 5. Figure 2. Analytical results (×) for the distribution of eccentricities P(E > ℓ) of nodes in RRGs that consist of nodes of degree c = 5 and network sizes of (a) N = 7, 500; (b) N = 10, 000; (c) N = 11, 000; (d) N = 12, 000; (e) N = 13, 000 and (f) N = 20, 000. The analytical results, obtained from Eq. (14), are in very good agreement with the results obtained from computer simulations (◦). The simulation results were averaged over 20 network instances. For N = 7, 500 the eccentricity of essentially all the nodes is E = 8. As N is increased, nodes of eccentricity E = 9 emerge and their weight increases until at N = 20, 000 essentially all the nodes are of eccentricity E = 9.

Figure 3. Analytical results (×) for the distribution of eccentricities P(E > ℓ) of nodes in RRGs that consist of nodes of degree c = 5 and network sizes of (a) N = 22, 000; (b) N = 36, 000; (c) N = 39, 000; (d) N = 41, 000; (e) N = 43, 000 and (f) N = 55, 000. The analytical results, obtained from Eq. (14), are in excellent agreement with the results obtained from computer simulations (◦). The simulation results were averaged over 20 network instances. For N = 22, 000 the eccentricity of essentially all the nodes is E = 9. As N is increased, nodes of eccentricity E = 10 emerge and their weight increases until at N = 55, 000 essentially all the nodes are of eccentricity E = 10.

Figure 4. Analytical results (×) for the probability (a) P(E > 5); (b) P(E > 8) and (c) P(E > 9), as a function of the network size N for RRGs consisting of nodes of degree c = 5, obtained from Eq. (14). The analytical results are found to be systematically larger than the corresponding simulation results (◦). For each value of ℓ, the probability P(E > ℓ) is shown for the window of network sizes in which it changes from zero to one. The discrepancy between the theory and simulation results decreases as the network size is increased.

Figure 5. Analytical results (×) and simulation results (◦) for the mean eccentricity ⟨E⟩in RRGs that consist of nodes of degree c = 5, as a function of the network size N. While the simulation results tend to lock in to integer values, the analytical results, obtained from Eq. (38), follow a smoothed-out contour. We also present approximate results (+), obtained from Eq. (40). These results, which are based on an approximate form of the tail-sum formula, are in very good agreement with the simulation results. However, the analytical expression given by Eq. (38) elucidates the scaling of ⟨E⟩as a function of N and c in a more transparent way.
